paragraphs: Text watermarking introduces a detectable pattern into generated language, but changing token choices can harm text quality. This paper develops an adaptive strategy intended to balance quality, robustness, and security while addressing the challenge of detection without prior knowledge of the prompt or generating model.

The method uses an auxiliary model to measure uncertainty in token distributions. It adds a watermark where entropy is high, meaning there is more flexibility in the next token, and leaves low-entropy distributions untouched. It also adjusts output scores using a semantic embedding of previously generated text. This replaces a fixed division of tokens into favored and disfavored lists with a mechanism conditioned on the text's meaning.

Experiments across several language models report robustness comparable to existing watermarking methods and perplexity comparable to generation without watermarks, while maintaining sufficient security. These findings support selectively placing the watermark where the model has room to vary its output. The reported security result is qualified; it does not establish immunity to every possible forgery or removal attempt.
icml-2024-adaptive-text-watermark-for-la.tldr: An adaptive watermark modifies uncertain token choices using semantic context, reporting comparable robustness with perplexity close to unwatermarked text.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn relationships between functions, including mappings used to predict solutions of partial differential equations. Many gain computational efficiency from the fast Fourier transform. Its reliance on evenly spaced rectangular grids becomes restrictive when the available measurements or desired outputs lie on irregularly distributed points.

The paper proposes evaluating the underlying spectral transformation directly. Its central observation is that a limited number of Fourier modes can provide the expressivity a neural operator needs. Working with this smaller collection makes direct spectral evaluation a practical route to handling arbitrary point distributions. The authors integrate an efficient implementation with existing neural operator models.

Extensive empirical evaluation reports substantial training-speed improvements over baselines while preserving or improving the accuracy of Fourier neural operators and related models. The contribution connects the representation a model actually uses to the computation it requires: if only a limited set of modes is needed, processing irregular points need not depend on the regular-grid machinery that originally made these models efficient.
icml-2024-beyond-regular-grids-fourier-b.tldr: Directly evaluating a limited set of Fourier modes extends neural operators to irregular point distributions with reported gains in training speed.

paragraphs: A bandit learner repeatedly selects actions and observes rewards. This paper also gives the learner additional variables after each action. When those variables separate the action from the reward in the relevant causal sense, prior results allow better worst-case regret rates. The challenge is to benefit from this favorable structure without knowing whether it exists.

The authors characterize the best achievable trade-offs between performance in favorable environments and performance in arbitrary ones. Their upper bounds describe attainable guarantees, while matching lower bounds establish the limits of improvement. Together, these results identify a Pareto frontier: the boundary of achievable combinations of the two types of performance.

The paper also reduces causal bandits to linear bandits to obtain bounds that depend on the particular problem instance. Finally, it examines the usual assumption that distributions of the post-action variables are known. It shows that a nontrivial estimate of these distributions is necessary to improve on worst-case minimax rates, making clear that exploiting causal structure also requires relevant distributional information.
icml-2024-causal-bandits-the-pareto-opti.tldr: The paper establishes optimal trade-offs for adapting bandit learning to unknown favorable causal structure and identifies necessary distributional information.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization spread across multiple nodes. Each node holds an objective that averages finitely many convex functions, and their combined global objective is strongly convex. The goal is to reduce the computation required at individual nodes while keeping the communication needed for cooperation competitive.

The proposed method uses stochastic gradients with variance reduction, improving the reliability of estimates built from subsets of local functions. It allows different nodes to use different mini-batch sizes in the same iteration. This flexibility is part of a first-order method designed for the decentralized finite-sum setting.

The theoretical computation-time bound depends on the global condition number, giving a sharper result than previous bounds based only on local condition numbers. The method also requires fewer local incremental first-order oracle calls while retaining comparable communication cost relative to state-of-the-art methods. Numerical experiments support its advantage. The result matters because an analysis based on the combined objective can give a more favorable account of difficulty than one governed only by the individual local objectives.
icml-2024-decentralized-convex-finite-su.tldr: A decentralized variance-reduced method improves computation bounds through global conditioning while allowing node-specific mini-batch sizes.

paragraphs: Aligning a language model with human preferences involves balancing two goals: increasing its preference reward and keeping its behavior close to the unaligned model. The second goal acts as a restraint on how far alignment can change the model. Choosing the strength of that restraint is an important part of the alignment process.

Too little restraint can allow reward hacking, where the model pursues reward in ways that can reduce its capabilities. Too much restraint can prevent useful alignment changes. Traditionally, exploring this balance requires training multiple models with different regularization strengths, which consumes substantial resources for large models.

The paper introduces decoding-time realignment, or DeRa, to explore different regularization strengths without retraining. It provides control while the model generates text, allowing users to move smoothly between unaligned and aligned behavior. This makes the degree of alignment adjustable during generation rather than requiring a new training run for each strength being evaluated.

DeRa also supports selecting effective regularization strengths with a validation dataset. Its stated contribution is a more efficient way to investigate the alignment tradeoff and tune that choice. The practical significance is the ability to evaluate different degrees of alignment while avoiding the repeated training that traditional tuning requires.
icml-2024-decoding-time-realignment-of-l.tldr: DeRa lets users adjust and evaluate a language model’s degree of alignment during decoding, making regularization tuning possible without retraining.

paragraphs: Deep equilibrium models are implicit neural networks, and their relationship to ordinary explicit networks is not fully understood. This paper investigates that relationship through two mathematical descriptions of network behavior: the conjugate kernel and the neural tangent kernel. It focuses on the eigenvalue patterns of their matrices.

Using random matrix theory, the authors analyze inputs drawn from a high-dimensional Gaussian mixture. In this setting, they prove that the kernels' spectral behavior depends on activation functions and initial weight variances through a system of just four nonlinear equations. This provides a compact description of how those design choices influence the analyzed kernels.

The result enables a carefully designed shallow explicit network to reproduce the conjugate kernel or neural tangent kernel of a given equilibrium model. The equivalence concerns these kernel descriptions, rather than an unrestricted identity between all aspects of the networks. Although the theory is derived for Gaussian-mixture inputs, experiments on popular real-world datasets support the broader usefulness of its analysis and design principles.
icml-2024-deep-equilibrium-models-are-al.tldr: For high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures, a compact kernel analysis shows how shallow explicit networks can match key kernels of deep equilibrium models.

paragraphs: DIDI learns a collection of skills from an existing mixture of behavioral data without requiring skill labels. Its objective combines two demands: the learned behaviors should differ meaningfully from one another, and they should remain similar to behavior represented in the offline data. Diversity alone would not express both goals.

The method uses diffusion probabilistic models as priors that guide learning and regularize the policy. A joint objective combines this guidance with a diversity objective. The diffusion component supplies a connection to the observed behavioral distribution, while the diversity component encourages the policy to develop distinguishable skills within that learning process.

Experiments in Push, Kitchen, Humanoid, and D4RL tasks show effective discovery of diverse, discriminative skills. The authors also introduce skill stitching and interpolation to demonstrate flexibility in the learned skill space. Adding an external reward function enables reward-guided generation, which the paper presents as a way to learn diverse and optimal behaviors from suboptimal data. The approach therefore supports both unlabeled skill discovery and generation directed by a specified reward.
icml-2024-didi-diffusion-guided-diversit.tldr: DIDI combines diffusion-based guidance with a diversity objective to learn distinct skills from unlabeled offline behavior.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer potential energy-efficiency and interpretability advantages, but they remain vulnerable to adversarial perturbations. This paper starts from an observation about that vulnerability: the networks tolerate random perturbations better than deliberately adversarial ones, even when the random changes are larger. The authors aim to narrow this performance gap.

Their analysis connects the gap to the input gradient of the probability assigned to the true label. This gradient describes how that probability responds to changes in the input image. They prove an upper bound on the gap involving gradient sparsity, providing a theoretical basis for a training strategy that regularizes this property.

The resulting method adds gradient sparsity regularization to improve robustness. Experiments on both image-based and event-based datasets report notable improvements, supporting the usefulness of the theoretical connection in practical training. The contribution links a measurable aspect of input sensitivity to the difference between random and adversarial disturbances, then uses that link to shape how spiking networks learn.
icml-2024-enhancing-adversarial-robustne.tldr: Gradient sparsity regularization improves spiking-network robustness, motivated by a bound connecting gradient sparsity to the random-versus-adversarial performance gap.

paragraphs: High-resolution salient object detection needs to locate prominent objects while preserving fine details. Processing a large image also raises computational cost. ESNet addresses these demands with a two-stage design that distributes localization and high-resolution refinement across different parts of the network.

The first stage uses a low-resolution location model. Mechanisms acting on supervision and features help it retain detail-relevant information while finding salient objects. The second stage inherits those features and supplements them with shallow features from the high-resolution image. This lightweight refinement produces the final high-resolution saliency prediction without assigning all of the work to a single high-resolution stage.

The paper also introduces Boundary-Detail-aware Mean Absolute Error, a metric intended to evaluate detail detection in high-resolution scenes. Across five datasets, the authors report superior performance relative to state-of-the-art methods at a real-time speed of 49 frames per second. The combined contribution addresses both prediction and evaluation: a staged model preserves details efficiently, while the proposed metric specifically assesses the detail quality that motivates the architecture.
icml-2024-esnet-evolution-and-succession.tldr: ESNet combines low-resolution localization with lightweight high-resolution refinement, reporting strong detail preservation and real-time salient object detection.

paragraphs: Graph signal denoising seeks to recover useful information associated with graph nodes despite noise. This paper reformulates the problem to account for perturbations of the graph structure itself. The motivation is that a graph-processing method must handle both unreliable node features and changes to the connections through which information is processed.

The authors introduce a min-max optimization problem. The maximization step perturbs the structure using Laplacian distance to increase the second term of the denoising objective. The minimization step then reduces the overall loss. Solving this formulation yields Graph Adversarial Diffusion Convolution, a variant of Graph Diffusion Convolution with an additional robustness-enhancing term.

The paper reports that this term improves resistance to adversarial changes in graph structure and noise in node features. It also improves the original diffusion method's performance on heterophilic graphs, and experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution is a connection between a robust denoising objective and a concrete diffusion architecture: the added architectural term follows from explicitly incorporating structural perturbations into the optimization problem.
icml-2024-graph-adversarial-diffusion-co.tldr: A min-max graph-denoising formulation produces a diffusion architecture that improves robustness to structural attacks and noisy node features.

paragraphs: Graph distillation compresses a large graph into a small synthetic graph that can support comparable graph-neural-network training performance. Existing approaches often supervise this process using a network's gradients, representations, or training trajectory. The paper argues that such supervision can bias the synthetic graph's spectrum and make the result depend on the chosen network architecture.

Graph Distillation with Eigenbasis Matching instead aligns the eigenbasis and node features of the real and synthetic graphs. It directly copies the real graph's spectrum, avoiding the influence of a supervising graph neural network on that component. A discrimination constraint is added to balance effectiveness and generalization.

The authors theoretically characterize the resulting synthetic graphs as restricted spectral approximations of their source graphs. Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art distillation methods, strong generalization across network architectures, and substantial distillation efficiency. These findings support using properties of the graph itself as the compression target, reducing dependence on the particular network used to guide or evaluate the distillation process.
icml-2024-graph-distillation-with-eigenb.tldr: GDEM distills graphs by matching spectral structure and node features, reporting efficient compression that generalizes across graph-network architectures.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn physical behavior from data, but some properties of a system may already be known. Conservation laws are a central example. If a model must discover these laws solely from finite, noisy observations, its predictions may satisfy them only approximately, even when the underlying physical system obeys them exactly.

The paper introduces conservation law-encoded neural operators, or clawNOs, that automatically satisfy the encoded conservation laws during inference. Their construction uses a divergence-free prediction of the solution field, which guarantees the continuity equation. This makes the relevant physical constraint a property of the prediction mechanism rather than something that must be recovered entirely from examples.

The authors demonstrate the approach in material-deformation modeling, incompressible fluid dynamics, and atmospheric simulation. They report substantial improvements in learning efficacy over state-of-the-art neural operators, especially with small datasets. The findings indicate that incorporating known physical structure can make data-driven learning more effective, while ensuring consistency with the conservation relationships represented by the construction.
icml-2024-harnessing-the-power-of-neural.tldr: ClawNOs build conservation constraints into neural-operator predictions and report improved learning, particularly when training data are limited.

paragraphs: An equivariant network changes its output in a prescribed way when its input undergoes a corresponding transformation. Lie Neurons builds this behavior for data in any finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra, where the associated group transforms the input through its adjoint action. This gives the network a symmetry requirement tailored to those mathematical spaces.

The framework extends Vector Neurons, which handles rotation symmetry in three-dimensional Euclidean space. Its construction uses the invariance of the Killing form to move beyond that original setting. New Lie bracket layers and geometric channel-mixing layers expand the modeling capacity while remaining within the proposed equivariant framework.

Experiments cover the so(3), sl(3), and sp(4) Lie algebras. Tasks include fitting invariant and equivariant functions, learning system dynamics, registering point clouds, and classifying shapes using homographies. The reported competitive performance across these tasks supports the framework's broad applicability. Its main contribution is a common network design for a larger class of structured inputs, with architectural operations built around the transformations those inputs naturally admit.
icml-2024-lie-neurons-adjoint-equivarian.tldr: Lie Neurons extends symmetry-respecting neural networks to finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebras, with competitive results across several geometric tasks.

paragraphs: Membership inference attacks try to determine whether a particular example was part of a model's training set. One defense strategy increases the variance of losses on training examples. Previous work has used gradient ascent for this purpose, but the paper argues that reversing the optimization direction can cause parameter oscillation and undermine training stability and performance.

Convex Concave Loss, or CCL, aims to obtain high training-loss variance while continuing to use gradient descent. The method follows theoretical analysis showing that convex losses tend to reduce loss variance during training. It adds a concave term to reduce the loss function's convexity, changing how ordinary descent shapes the distribution of training losses.

Experiments report that networks trained with CCL retain high loss variance and provide stronger defenses against membership inference attacks. The authors describe the resulting privacy-utility balance as state of the art. The contribution concerns both the privacy objective and the optimization procedure: it pursues a protective loss distribution through a modified training loss, avoiding the instability associated with the ascent-based approach discussed in the paper.
icml-2024-mitigating-privacy-risk-in-mem.tldr: CCL adds a concave loss term to increase training-loss variance through gradient descent and improve the reported privacy-utility balance.

paragraphs: Bootstrap methods simulate uncertainty arising from input data, but their computational cost can become substantial when the sample count is large. Orthogonal Bootstrap targets the number of Monte Carlo replications needed for this simulation. The goal is to obtain a useful uncertainty assessment with less repeated computational work.

The method decomposes the quantity being simulated into two components. The non-orthogonal component has a closed-form result given by the Infinitesimal Jackknife, so that contribution can be handled analytically. The remaining orthogonal component is easier to simulate. This division concentrates Monte Carlo effort on the part that still needs it.

Theoretical and numerical results show a significant reduction in bootstrap computation. The paper also reports improved empirical accuracy while maintaining the width of the constructed interval. That combination matters because the computational saving is accompanied by a more accurate empirical result without changing interval width. The central contribution is the decomposition itself: using an available analytic calculation changes what must be simulated and reduces the replication burden.
icml-2024-orthogonal-bootstrap-efficient.tldr: Orthogonal Bootstrap combines an analytic component with an easier simulation problem to reduce computation while improving empirical accuracy.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning relies on judgments about which behaviors are preferable, and collecting those labels can be expensive. PEARL aims to reuse preferences from other tasks to learn a target-task policy without human preference labels for that target. Its zero-shot claim concerns this transfer of preference supervision.

Cross-task Preference Alignment uses optimal transport to establish correspondences between trajectories from different tasks. Specifically, a Gromov-Wasserstein distance guides the alignment, and the resulting transport matrix provides correspondence weights. Target-task preferences are then calculated as weighted combinations of source-task preference labels, turning the alignment into usable supervision.

A second component, Robust Reward Learning, models rewards as Gaussian distributions so learning considers both reward means and uncertainty. This addresses the need to learn robustly from transferred labels. Experiments on robotic manipulation tasks in Meta-World and Robomimic report accurate preference transfer and well-behaved learned policies, with particularly strong advantages when human preferences are scarce. Together, the components connect cross-task correspondence with uncertainty-aware reward learning.
icml-2024-pearl-zero-shot-cross-task-pre.tldr: PEARL transfers preferences between robotic tasks and learns uncertainty-aware rewards without collecting human preference labels for the target task.

paragraphs: In performative prediction, deploying a predictor changes the distribution of future observations. A useful predictor therefore needs to perform well on the distribution its own deployment creates. Optimizing this performative risk requires accounting for the feedback between a model's predictions and the data it subsequently encounters.

The paper studies a middle ground between two existing approaches. Model-agnostic methods can avoid assumptions about the feedback but converge very slowly. Explicit feedback models can enable faster learning, yet their rate guarantees critically depend on the models being correct. Plug-in performative optimization provides a general protocol for using feedback models that may be misspecified.

The authors show that this protocol can substantially outperform model-agnostic strategies when misspecification is not too extreme. The qualification is central: the result supports the usefulness of imperfect models under controlled error, rather than claiming every inaccurate model helps. It gives a theoretical reason to exploit partial understanding of performative feedback instead of treating exact correctness as the only basis for using a model.
icml-2024-plug-in-performative-optimizat.tldr: Plug-in performative optimization can outperform model-agnostic learning when its feedback model is imperfect but not too severely misspecified.

paragraphs: AutoML began with several ambitions: configuring machine-learning workflows automatically and efficiently, supporting research into new algorithms, and making machine learning accessible to more people. This position paper argues that progress has concentrated heavily on predictive performance, leaving open how fully the field has served those broader purposes.

The authors identify interaction between people and AutoML systems as an underexplored research priority. Users bring different roles, expectations, and levels of expertise, so improving a system's predictions alone does not address the full range of ways people need to work with it. Their proposal places those differences at the center of future research.

The envisioned approach treats machine-learning system design as a collaboration between human expertise and automated methods. Its significance is a proposed change in what AutoML research pays attention to: useful automation includes how people contribute to and interact with the resulting workflow. As a position paper, it offers an argument and research direction, rather than reporting an experimental demonstration that a particular interface or collaboration method has solved these challenges.
icml-2024-position-a-call-to-action-for-.tldr: The paper argues that AutoML should prioritize human interaction and collaborative design alongside predictive performance.

paragraphs: PPFlow addresses the design of therapeutic peptides with a particular protein target in view. The paper focuses on generating peptide structures, an area the authors describe as insufficiently explored in AI-assisted drug discovery. Its approach models internal peptide geometry through torsion angles, making these structural variables central to the design process.

The model uses conditional flow matching on torus manifolds to represent those angles. This mathematical setting accommodates their angular geometry and provides the basis for target-aware structure generation. Alongside the method, the authors introduce PPBench2024, a protein-peptide binding dataset intended to support deep-learning training for structure-based peptide drug design.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance against baseline models on peptide generation and optimization. The authors also report that the approach generalizes to docking and side-chain packing, extending its use beyond the primary design tasks. The contribution combines a geometry-focused generative method with a dataset for learning protein-peptide relationships. Its reported findings establish computational performance on these tasks; the therapeutic motivation is the reason for pursuing the design problem.
icml-2024-ppflow-target-aware-peptide-de.tldr: PPFlow models peptide torsion angles with target-conditioned flow matching and introduces a binding dataset, reporting strong generation and optimization results.

paragraphs: Machine-learning approaches to synthesis planning often combine one-step retrosynthesis predictions with a search procedure that works backward from the desired molecule. The paper identifies a weakness in choosing the next molecule set greedily: a locally attractive choice does not account for the quality of the full route. Existing strategies also lack control based on criteria such as material costs, yields, and step count.

The proposed framework uses conditional residual energy-based models to assess entire synthetic routes according to specified criteria. An additional energy function modifies the probabilistic model so that route-level quality influences which routes receive high probability. The framework is designed to be added to different generation strategies in a plug-and-play manner.

Extensive experiments report consistent performance gains across multiple strategies and a 2.5% margin over the previous state-of-the-art top-1 accuracy. The broader contribution is a way to incorporate whole-route preferences into synthesis planning. It allows the probabilistic ranking of routes to reflect criteria beyond the immediate next retrosynthesis choice.
icml-2024-preference-optimization-for-mo.tldr: A conditional residual energy model improves synthesis-route generation by incorporating preferences about the quality of the entire route.

paragraphs: A narrow neural network can use very few units in each layer while still approximating a broad class of functions. Earlier work established that width d+1 suffices to approximate any continuous function arbitrarily well for input dimension d. This paper asks a sharper question: how efficiently can such a network reduce approximation error as its number of tunable parameters grows?

The authors prove that ReLU networks of width d+1 achieve the optimal approximation rate for continuous functions on the unit cube under Lp norms for finite p at least one. These norms assess approximation error differently from the uniform norm, which controls the largest error across the domain. For the uniform norm, the paper proves that width d+11 is sufficient.

The results also extend to narrow feed-forward networks with several other activation functions. They strengthen universal approximation statements by addressing the relationship between parameter count and error. The width d+11 result is a sufficiency claim; it does not establish that every network achieving the uniform-norm rate must have that width.
icml-2024-relu-network-with-width-d-math.tldr: Narrow ReLU networks achieve optimal approximation rates at width d+1 for finite Lp norms, while width d+11 suffices for the uniform norm.

paragraphs: Probabilistic circuits are generative models that permit exact, efficient probabilistic inference on the distributions they learn. Their practical scale can still be limited by the time and memory costs of software implementations. PyJuice addresses this systems bottleneck with a general GPU implementation design for training larger circuits.

Its core is a compilation process that translates a circuit into a compact representation suited to block-based parallel computation. This reduces data movement and enables use of modern GPUs' Tensor Cores. The paper reports training speedups of one to two orders of magnitude over existing systems, together with two to five times lower GPU memory consumption.

Those savings allow larger models to be trained. Experiments use PyJuice to improve state-of-the-art probabilistic circuits on image and language datasets, including ImageNet32, WikiText, and CommonGen. The authors also establish baselines using existing circuit structures at larger sizes and with more training epochs. The contribution shows how implementation efficiency can expand the modeling scale available to a framework whose appeal already includes tractable inference.
icml-2024-scaling-tractable-probabilisti.tldr: PyJuice compiles probabilistic circuits for efficient GPU execution, reporting major training speedups and lower memory use that enable larger models.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction expresses uncertainty through prediction sets, whose informativeness depends in part on their size. This paper investigates how those sets behave under adversarial attacks. It finds that existing conformal methods do not produce informative sets under the studied infinity-norm-bounded attacks when the underlying model lacks adversarial training.

Adversarial training helps, but the authors find that variants of it often produce worse prediction-set sizes than standard adversarial training. This motivates Uncertainty-Reducing Adversarial Training, or AT-UR, which explicitly targets conformal efficiency. Its objective combines a Beta-weighting loss with an entropy-minimization regularizer during training.

The theoretical analysis shows that the Beta-weighting loss upper-bounds prediction-set size at the population level. This provides a mathematical connection between the training objective and the uncertainty representation the authors want to improve. Experiments on four image-classification datasets across three adversarial-training baselines support the method's effectiveness. The findings make prediction-set size an explicit consideration in robust model training, alongside the protection against attacks that motivates adversarial training itself.
icml-2024-the-pitfalls-and-promise-of-co.tldr: AT-UR modifies adversarial training to improve conformal prediction-set sizes, supported by a population-level bound and image-classification experiments.

paragraphs: Image restoration, enhancement, and feature extraction are often handled by separate models requiring task-specific design expertise. PromptGIP brings these low-level vision tasks into a shared model. It follows the broader idea of using pretraining and in-context examples to specify what a model should do.

The framework treats an input-output image pair as a structured question and answer. Visual prompts then communicate the desired image-processing operation, turning task execution into a visual question-answering problem. This lets the same model undertake different tasks across domains without task-specific fine-tuning.

The authors report that PromptGIP can handle up to 15 image-processing tasks. They also observe some generalization to tasks outside the training domain, while explicitly leaving stronger emergent generalization for further investigation. The main contribution is the common task interface: examples of image transformations become a way to direct one model across diverse processing operations. The stated out-of-domain result supports a degree of adaptability, rather than establishing that arbitrary new image-processing tasks can be solved.
icml-2024-unifying-image-processing-as-v.tldr: PromptGIP uses visual question-answer examples to direct one model across up to 15 image-processing tasks without task-specific fine-tuning.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic optimization when an objective is nonconvex and nonsmooth and the solution must remain in a closed convex set. These features complicate both algorithm design and the definition of progress. Much earlier work transforms the constrained problem into an unconstrained one but supplies only asymptotic convergence analysis.

The authors first generalize two measures used to assess stationarity: gradient mapping and the Frank-Wolfe gap. Their extensions apply to the nonsmooth setting and support new definitions of approximate stationarity. These definitions provide explicit targets for evaluating whether an algorithm has reached a point that satisfies the proposed stopping criterion.

The paper then develops several stochastic zeroth-order algorithms, which use function evaluations rather than requiring gradient access, and proves non-asymptotic guarantees for reaching those targets. Numerical experiments demonstrate their effectiveness. The central advance is a finite-time theoretical treatment tied to measures suitable for the constrained nonsmooth problem. The guarantees concern approximate stationarity, preserving the distinction between a stationarity result and a claim to find a global optimum.
icml-2024-zeroth-order-methods-for-const.tldr: New stationarity measures support zeroth-order algorithms with finite-time guarantees for constrained, nonconvex, nonsmooth stochastic optimization.
